title: Brazil’s Far-Right Resurgence
gist: Flávio Bolsonaro beat Lula 47.03% to 45.16% in Brazil's first round, defying polls, and his Liberal Party expanded in Congress and governorships, making a Bolsonaro return likely in the Oct. 25 runoff given that no first-round loser has won a runoff since redemocratization. The brief also covers Panama's 'reopen to close' plan for a copper mine that supplied ~1.5% of global output, Chilean President Kast's 60% disapproval, and an OAS escalation against Nicaragua.

insights.claim: Contrary to most polls showing Lula narrowly ahead, Flávio Bolsonaro won Brazil's first-round presidential vote with 47.03 percent to Lula's 45.16 percent, setting up an Oct. 25 runoff.
insights.so_what: A likely right-wing, pro-business presidency is a major catalyst for Brazilian equities, the real, and fiscal expectations.
insights.quote: By the time all votes were counted, Bolsonaro had earned 47.03 percent to Lula’s 45.16 percent.
insights.locator: By the time all votes were counted
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn

insights.claim: History favors Bolsonaro in the runoff: no Brazilian presidential candidate since 1980s redemocratization has won a runoff after losing the first round, and the third-, fourth-, and fifth-place finishers were all right-wing.
insights.so_what: Markets should price a high probability of a Bolsonaro presidency from 2027.
insights.quote: No presidential candidate since Brazil’s redemocratization in the 1980s has won a runoff election after losing in the first round.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn

insights.claim: Bolsonaro's Liberal Party won the most governorships settled in the first round and grew in both houses of Congress, remaining the largest party in each while ousting several center-right lawmakers.
insights.so_what: A stronger congressional base would let a Bolsonaro government pass its agenda more easily than Lula's coalition could.
insights.quote: The Liberal Party booted several center-right lawmakers out of office Sunday, furthering its takeover of the Brazilian right.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn

insights.claim: Quaest pollster Felipe Nunes's analysis suggests many voters who intended to back minor right-wing candidates switched to Bolsonaro to try to win in the first round, explaining the polling miss.
insights.so_what: Tactical consolidation on the right suggests Brazilian polls may understate right-wing support.
insights.locator: Bolsonaro and Lula are now headed
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn

insights.claim: Lula performed worse among lower-middle-class Brazilians, many of them evangelical gig workers on city outskirts, than among the richest, reflecting his party's failure to understand a class his own anti-poverty policies helped create.
insights.so_what: The political realignment of Brazil's gig-economy lower middle class favors deregulatory, pro-security policy.
insights.quote: Demographic data shows he performed worse on Sunday among lower-middle-class Brazilians than among the richest.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn

insights.claim: Lula's new tough-on-crime slogan implicitly concedes that the right dominates messaging on insecurity, while his push to outlaw six-day workweek contracts has about 70 percent support but does not cover gig workers.
insights.so_what: Labor-market regulation proposals remain a campaign lever affecting Brazilian employers if Lula recovers.
insights.quote: “For working people, protection; for criminals, jail.”
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn

insights.claim: Lula admitted his campaign was the least organized he had participated in since 1989.
insights.so_what: Self-acknowledged campaign weakness reinforces the odds of a Bolsonaro win.
insights.quote: his campaign “was the least organized I’ve participated in since 1989 and we reaped what we sowed.”
insights.locator: Offering another hypothesis for the results
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn

insights.claim: Bolsonaro has campaigned on broad pro-change, pro-business, and pro-security ideas without policy detail, which has not yet hurt him with voters.
insights.so_what: Lack of policy specifics leaves uncertainty about fiscal and economic plans despite a market-friendly tone.
insights.quote: His lack of details hasn’t turned off voters—so far.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn

insights.claim: A Panamanian government panel recommended a 'reopen to close' plan for the giant copper mine shut after 2023 protests, a phaseout analysts say could take 25 years; the mine supplied about 1.5 percent of global copper before closing.
insights.so_what: A restart would add meaningful copper supply to a tight market and restore Panama as a critical-minerals supplier.
insights.quote: a commercial asset that accounted for around 1.5 percent of global copper production prior to its closure
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn

insights.claim: Environmental groups reacted to the Panama mine phaseout plan with skepticism but no immediate protests, suggesting the plan could be a viable path to reactivation.
insights.so_what: Muted opposition lowers execution risk for the mine restart.
insights.locator: Such a phaseout could reasonably take
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn

insights.claim: Chilean President José Antonio Kast has a 60 percent disapproval rating seven months into his term, with Iran-war fuel prices compounding the pain of his public spending cuts, and 47 percent of informed Chileans rejecting his decision to join Trump's Shield of the Americas versus 31 percent supporting.
insights.so_what: Austerity plus energy-price shocks is eroding support for Latin America's new right governments, a political risk for reform agendas.
insights.quote: he has a 60 percent disapproval rate, according to the same poll
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn

insights.claim: Former Chilean presidents Gabriel Boric and Michelle Bachelet jointly argued Chile should not pick a side in great-power competition, signaling a left-wing comeback effort.
insights.so_what: Points to a potential policy swing back toward nonalignment in Chile's future politics.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn

insights.claim: The OAS unanimously set eight demands for Nicaragua, including releasing political prisoners and moving toward elections, and will reconvene within 120 days to consider punitive measures, possibly economic penalties, if nothing changes.
insights.so_what: Possible regional economic sanctions on Nicaragua could affect trade and investment exposure there.
insights.quote: to reconvene in up to 120 days to consider applying unspecified punitive measures (excluding military force)
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn

insights.claim: The Trump administration backed a collective OAS approach to Nicaragua, unlike its unilateral actions on Cuba and Venezuela, because Nicaragua lacks Cuba's domestic political weight and Venezuela's oil reserves.
insights.so_what: US unilateral intervention in Latin America tracks oil and domestic political stakes, a useful guide for assessing regional risk.
insights.quote: Nicaragua, however, does not loom as large as Cuba in U.S. domestic politics, nor does it hold major oil reserves like Venezuela.
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn

insights.claim: BTS's current tour visits more Latin American countries and cities than Taylor Swift's 2023-24 Eras Tour, reflecting Korean music's rise in a region that has traditionally looked to the US or Europe culturally.
insights.so_what: Latin America is a growing market for Korean entertainment exports and soft power.
insights.quote: The current BTS tour is visiting more Latin American countries and cities than Taylor Swift’s 2023-24 Eras Tour
insights.locator: The current BTS tour is visiting
insights.speaker: Catherine Osborn
